expectedText:
ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION (CALIFORNIA CORPORATION)
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION DECLARATION
The name of the corporation is Acme, Inc. The purpose of Acme, Inc. is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the General Corporation Law of California, other than the banking business, the trust company business, or the practice of a profession that California law requires to be separately incorporated. Acme, Inc. is authorized to issue 10,000,000 shares of stock. The initial street address of Acme, Inc.'s principal office is 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105.

CORPORATE EXISTENCE BEGINS UPON FILING
A California corporation may be formed by one or more natural persons, partnerships, associations, or corporations (domestic or foreign) who execute and file articles of incorporation with the Secretary of State. Corporate existence begins the moment the articles are filed — not on any earlier date the incorporators sign the document — and continues perpetually unless the law or the articles themselves provide otherwise. If the articles name the corporation's initial directors, each of those directors must personally sign and acknowledge the articles; if no initial directors are named, the articles are instead signed by the person or persons forming the corporation, who are then the incorporators.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "One or more natural persons, partnerships, associations or corporations, domestic or foreign, may form a corporation under this division by executing and filing articles of incorporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 200(a), California General Corporation Law, who may form a corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=200.)
  "If initial directors are named in the articles, each director named in the articles shall sign and acknowledge the articles; if initial directors are not named in the articles, the articles shall be signed by one or more persons described in subdivision (a) who thereupon are the incorporators of the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 200(b), California General Corporation Law, who signs the articles (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=200.)
  "The corporate existence begins upon the filing of the articles and continues perpetually, unless otherwise expressly provided by law or in the articles."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 200(c), California General Corporation Law, the moment corporate existence begins (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=200.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who may form a corporation and when a corporation's legal existence begins — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's formation; who may form a corporation, and the moment its existence begins, vary by state. All three quotes below come from subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 200, so they are treated as one source, not three independent ones.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF THE ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION
California's articles-of-incorporation statute requires the filed document to state: the corporation's name; one of two alternative purpose statements — either the general default that the corporation's purpose is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the General Corporation Law (other than the banking business, the trust-company business, or the practice of a licensed profession), or, for a corporation formed to practice a specific licensed profession, a statement naming that profession; the name and California street address of the corporation's initial agent for service of process; the initial street address of the corporation's principal office, plus a separate mailing address if it differs; and, because a California corporation exists by default as a stock corporation, a statement of its initial share structure — either the total number of shares authorized (if only one class of stock), or, if more than one class or series is authorized, the number, designation, and rights of each class and series.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The name of the corporation; provided, however, that in order for the corporation to be subject to the provisions of this division applicable to a close corporation (Section 158), the name of the corporation must contain the word “corporation,” “incorporated,” or “limited” or an abbreviation of one of such words."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 202(a), California General Corporation Law, the corporation's name (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=202.)
  "The purpose of the corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the General Corporation Law of California other than the banking business, the trust company business or the practice of a profession permitted to be incorporated by the California Corporations Code"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 202(b)(1)(A), California General Corporation Law, the default lawful-purpose statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=202.)
  "(c) The name and street address in this state of the corporation’s initial agent for service of process in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 1502. (d) The initial street address of its principal office. (e) The initial mailing address of the corporation, if different from the initial street address."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 202(c)-(e), California General Corporation Law, agent for service of process and office addresses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=202.)
  "If the corporation is authorized to issue only one class of shares, the total number of shares which the corporation is authorized to issue."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 202(f), California General Corporation Law, initial authorized shares (single-class corporations) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=202.)
  Known gap: This is one state's list of required formation-document content, not a claim about what any other state's equivalent filing must contain — required content for a corporation's founding filing varies by state. The four citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 202, so they are treated as one source, not four independent ones; no additional independent source was found for this.

THE CORPORATION NAME REQUIREMENT
California's general naming statute for corporations does not, by default, require a corporation's name to include any particular word like "Corporation," "Incorporated," "Limited," or an abbreviation of one of those words — that designator requirement applies only to a corporation that elects to be governed by the state's close-corporation provisions. What the general naming statute actually restricts is different: the Secretary of State will not file articles using a name containing "bank," "trust," "trustee," or related words unless a specified financial regulator's certificate of approval is attached, and separately, a corporation's name cannot be one the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public, or that isn't distinguishable in the Secretary of State's records from other registered or reserved entity names.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The Secretary of State shall not file articles setting forth a name in which “bank,” “ trust,” “trustee,” or related words appear, unless the certificate of approval of the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation is attached thereto."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 201(a), California General Corporation Law, the bank/trust name restriction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=201.)
  "The name of a corporation shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public and shall be distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State from all of the following: (1) The name of any corporation. (2) The name of any foreign corporation authorized to transact intrastate business in this state."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 201(b), California General Corporation Law, the misleading-name and distinguishability requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=201.)
  "The name of the corporation; provided, however, that in order for the corporation to be subject to the provisions of this division applicable to a close corporation (Section 158), the name of the corporation must contain the word “corporation,” “incorporated,” or “limited” or an abbreviation of one of such words."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 202(a), California General Corporation Law, the designator requirement is close-corporation-specific (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=202.)
  Known gap: This is one state's naming statute, not a claim about naming rules in any other state — restricted words, and whether any designator word must be included in an entity's name at all, vary by state. This is also a genuine correction to an assumption worth stating plainly: unlike California's LLC-naming statute (which requires every LLC's name to include "limited liability company," "LLC," or "L.L.C."), the general California corporation-naming statute does not require any designator word in the name of an ordinary corporation — the "corporation," "incorporated," or "limited" designator is mandatory only for a corporation that has elected close-corporation status, not for corporations generally. The quotes below draw from two independently enacted sections: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(a) and § 201(b) are subsections of one section and are treated as one source; Cal. Corp. Code § 202(a) (quoted again here specifically for its close-corporation designator caveat) is an independently verified second source.

CORPORATE AGENT FOR SERVICE OF PROCESS DESIGNATION
The name of Acme, Inc.'s initial agent for service of process in California is Jordan Alex Lee. The agent's street address in California is 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105.

DESIGNATING AN AGENT FOR SERVICE OF PROCESS
Every corporation's articles of incorporation must name an initial agent for service of process along with that agent's California street address, meeting the qualifications set out in the state's Statement of Information statute. That statute requires the agent to be either a natural person residing in California — whose complete business or residence street address must be stated — or a corporation that has separately qualified to act as a registered corporate agent, in which case no address for that corporate agent is included in the filing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The name and street address in this state of the corporation’s initial agent for service of process in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 1502."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 202(c), California General Corporation Law, agent for service of process named in the articles (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=202.)
  "The statement required by subdivision (a) shall also designate, as the agent of the corporation for the purpose of service of process, a natural person residing in this state or a corporation that has complied with Section 1505 and whose capacity to act as an agent has not terminated. If a natural person is designated, the statement shall set forth that person’s complete business or residence street address. If a corporate agent is designated, no address for it shall be set forth."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1502(b), California General Corporation Law, who may serve as agent for service of process (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1502.)
  Known gap: This is one state's agent-for-service-of-process requirement for corporations, not a claim about what any other state requires — whether a corporation must maintain an in-state agent at all, and who may serve as one, varies by state. Unlike California's LLC statute, which contains an explicit freestanding sentence requiring an LLC to "designate and continuously maintain" an agent for service of process (Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.13(a)), this research did not find equivalently explicit "continuously maintain" language written for corporations; the corporation-specific duty instead comes through indirectly, from the requirement that the initial articles name an agent and from the recurring Statement of Information filing that must re-designate one. The two quotes below come from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 202(c) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1502(b), so they are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section.

THE CORPORATION'S FOLLOW-UP STATEMENT OF INFORMATION
Filing articles of incorporation does not end a corporation's filing obligations to the state. California requires every corporation to file an initial statement of information with the Secretary of State within 90 days after its articles are filed, and then again every year thereafter during the corporation's assigned filing period (or, if nothing has changed, to certify that no changes have occurred in lieu of refiling). The statement must report the corporation's name and Secretary of State file number, the names and addresses of its incumbent directors and any board vacancies, the names and addresses of its chief executive officer, secretary, and chief financial officer, its principal and mailing office addresses, the general type of business it conducts, its current agent for service of process, and a disclosure of whether any officer or director has an outstanding, non-appealable wage-order or Labor Code judgment against them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Every corporation shall file, within 90 days after the filing of its original articles and annually thereafter during the applicable filing period, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State, a statement containing all of the following: (1) The name of the corporation and the Secretary of State’s file number. (2) The names and complete business or residence addresses of its incumbent directors. (3) The number of vacancies on the board, if any. (4) The names and complete business or residence addresses of its chief executive officer, secretary, and chief financial officer. (5) The street address of its principal executive office."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1502(a), California General Corporation Law, initial and annual statement of information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1502.)
  "For the purposes of this section, the applicable filing period for a corporation shall be the calendar month during which its original articles were filed and the immediately preceding five calendar months. The Secretary of State shall provide a notice to each corporation to comply with this section approximately three months prior to the close of the applicable filing period... The failure of the corporation to receive the notice is not an excuse for failure to comply with this section."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1502(d), California General Corporation Law, how the annual filing period is measured (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1502.)
  Known gap: This is one state's periodic-reporting requirement for corporations, not a claim about what any other state requires after formation — whether a follow-up report is required at all, and how often, varies by state. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 1502, and are treated as one source; no additional independent source was found for this. One distinction worth flagging precisely because this project's existing LLC Articles of Organization document describes a similar-sounding filing: the corporate version of this requirement recurs annually, while the parallel LLC statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.09) sets a biennial, every-two-year filing period — these are different cadences, and this corporate document should not be read as describing the LLC timeline.

THE ANNUAL MINIMUM FRANCHISE TAX
Incorporating in California also triggers a state tax obligation separate from the Secretary of State's filing fee. California's Revenue and Taxation Code subjects every corporation incorporated under California law to the state's minimum franchise tax — currently eight hundred dollars ($800) annually — running from the earlier of the date of incorporation, qualification, or first doing business in the state, until the corporation's dissolution or withdrawal becomes effective. Separately, that same statute exempts a newly incorporated corporation from the minimum franchise tax for its first taxable year, applicable to any corporation that incorporates or qualifies to do business in California on or after January 1, 2000 — with that first-year exemption expressly not extending to LLCs, limited partnerships, LLPs, or several other listed entity types.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Every corporation described in subdivision (b) shall be subject to the minimum franchise tax specified in subdivision (d) from the earlier of the date of incorporation, qualification, or commencing to do business within this state, until the effective date of dissolution or withdrawal as provided in Section 23331 or, if later, the date the corporation ceases to do business within the limits of this state."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(a), The Corporation Franchise Tax, when the minimum tax applies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23153.)
  "Except as provided in paragraph (2), paragraph (1) of subdivision (f) of Section 23151, paragraph (1) of subdivision (f) of Section 23181, and paragraph (1) of subdivision (c) of Section 23183, corporations subject to the minimum franchise tax shall pay annually to the state a minimum franchise tax of eight hundred dollars ($800)."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(d)(1), The Corporation Franchise Tax, the $800 minimum franchise tax amount (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23153.)
  "(1) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), every corporation that incorporates or qualifies to do business in this state on or after January 1, 2000, shall not be subject to the minimum franchise tax for its first taxable year. (2) This subdivision shall not apply to limited partnerships, as defined in Section 17935, limited liability companies, as defined in Section 17941, limited liability partnerships, as described in Section 17948, charitable organizations, as described in Section 23703, regulated investment companies, as defined in Section 851 of the Internal Revenue Code, real estate investment trusts, as defined in Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code, real estate mortgage investment conduits, as defined in Section 860D of the Internal Revenue Code, and qualified Subchapter S subsidiaries, as defined in Section 1361(b)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code, to the extent applicable."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(f)(1)-(2), The Corporation Franchise Tax, the permanent first-year exemption and its exclusions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23153.)
  Known gap: This is one state's minimum annual corporate tax, not a claim about what any other state charges — whether a state imposes a flat annual tax on corporations at all, and in what amount, varies by state. This clause also corrects an assumption worth checking rather than carrying over from this project's existing LLC research: the LLC Articles of Organization document describes a first-year exemption from the $800 minimum tax that was temporary, applying only to LLCs organizing between January 1, 2021 and January 1, 2024 (Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941(g)). The corporation first-year exemption verified here is a different, older provision found in effect as of this verification date with no stated end date in this section — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(f)(1), covering any corporation that incorporates or qualifies to do business in California on or after January 1, 2000. These are not the same exemption extended to a second entity type; they are separately worded, separately dated provisions in different statutory sections that happen to produce a similar-looking result, and by its own terms the corporate exemption does not reach LLCs or several other listed entity types. The three quotes below come from subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153, and are treated as one source, not three independent ones.

WHICH CORPORATIONS THE MINIMUM FRANCHISE TAX REACHES
Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(b) defines the corporations the minimum franchise tax reaches, unless expressly exempted elsewhere in the Corporation Tax Law or by the California Constitution: a corporation incorporated under California law, a corporation qualified to transact intrastate business in California under the Corporations Code, or a corporation doing business in California. Section 23153(c) then carves two entity types out of the tax entirely: credit unions, and a narrow category of agricultural nonprofit cooperative associations organized under the Food and Agricultural Code and holding a specified board-of-supervisors certificate, which are exempt for five consecutive taxable years starting with the year the certificate issued -- and only if the cooperative organized on or after January 1, 1994. Limited liability companies are not reached by this section directly; a separate statute, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941, imposes an annual LLC tax and cross-references subdivision (d) of this section only to set that tax's dollar amount.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Unless expressly exempted by this part or the California Constitution, subdivision (a) shall apply to each of the following: (1) Every corporation that is incorporated under the laws of this state. (2) Every corporation that is qualified to transact intrastate business in this state pursuant to Chapter 21 (commencing with Section 2100) of Division 1 of Title 1 of the Corporations Code. (3) Every corporation that is doing business in this state."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(b), The Corporation Franchise Tax, which corporations the minimum tax applies to (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23153.)
  "The following entities are not subject to the minimum franchise tax specified in this section: (1) Credit unions. (2) Nonprofit cooperative associations organized pursuant to Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 54001) of Division 20 of the Food and Agricultural Code that have been issued the certificate of the board of supervisors prepared pursuant to Section 54042 of the Food and Agricultural Code. The association shall be exempt from the minimum franchise tax for five consecutive taxable years, commencing with the first taxable year for which the certificate is issued pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 54042 of the Food and Agricultural Code. This paragraph only applies to nonprofit cooperative associations organized on or after January 1, 1994."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(c), The Corporation Franchise Tax, express exemptions for credit unions and certain agricultural cooperatives (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23153.)
  Known gap: Subdivisions (b) and (c) quoted here are further subsections of the same statutory section already partly quoted elsewhere in this project -- Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(a), (d)(1), and (f)(1)-(2) appear in the Articles of Incorporation document's annual-franchise-tax clause, and § 23153(d)(1) is separately cross-referenced in the LLC Articles of Organization document and the LLC Annual Fee document -- all one statutory source, not independent ones. This clause does not cover every subdivision of § 23153: it omits the reduced $25 rate for a narrow category of inactive pre-1950s gold-mining or pre-1971 quicksilver-mining corporations formed under California law (subdivision (d)(2)-(3)), an expired 1999-2000 reduced second-year rate for certain small newly incorporated corporations (subdivision (e)), an anti-abuse rule for reorganizations undertaken solely to avoid the tax (subdivision (f)(3)), a narrow dissolution-linked exemption tied to a since-amended Corporations Code filing procedure that is distinct from the currently operative dissolution relief mechanism this project verifies elsewhere as Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332(c) (subdivision (g)), and a small-business exemption for a corporation solely owned by a deployed member of the U.S. Armed Forces, operative for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2020 and becoming inoperative for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2030 (subdivision (i)) -- all left unaddressed here as narrow, historical, or niche provisions outside this clause's scope. This clause also does not address whether, or under what circumstances, an LLC that elects corporate tax treatment is itself treated as a "corporation" reached directly by § 23153(b) rather than by § 17941; the statutory text of § 23153 itself does not resolve that question, and no further source was fetched to verify it.

STATUTORY LIMIT ON RAISING THE $800 FIGURE
Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(h) caps how quickly the Legislature may raise the $800 minimum franchise tax figure set in subdivision (d)(1): the Legislature may not increase it by more than 10 percent during any calendar year. The $800 figure itself is therefore not fixed permanently by this section's text -- it is a ceiling on the rate of legislative increase, not a promise that the amount will stay at $800 indefinitely.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The minimum franchise tax imposed by paragraph (1) of subdivision (d) shall not be increased by the Legislature by more than 10 percent during any calendar year."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(h), The Corporation Franchise Tax, 10% annual cap on legislative increases to the minimum tax (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23153.)
  Known gap: This is a single subdivision of the same statutory section quoted elsewhere in this project, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153 -- one source, not an independent one. This clause states only the existence and terms of the statutory cap; it does not report whether the Legislature has exercised, or is currently proposing to exercise, this authority, and it does not track the tax's historical dollar amount before it reached $800.

DELAYED FILING AND DELAYED EFFECTIVE DATES
California's general corporate-filing statute gives a corporation two different, non-interchangeable ways to time when a filed document takes effect. First, under the ordinary filing-date rule, the person filing any instrument — including the original articles of incorporation — may ask the Secretary of State to withhold it from filing until a specified future date up to 90 days after the Secretary of State receives it, so long as the document actually arrives at least one business day before that requested date; if honored, the filing date itself becomes that later date. Second, and separately, the statute lets a corporation specify that an instrument is to become effective up to 90 days after its filing date, rather than immediately upon filing — but that second, 'delayed effective date' mechanism is expressly unavailable for original articles of incorporation; the statute limits it to instruments filed with respect to a corporation that already exists.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except for instruments filed pursuant to Section 1502, the date of filing shall be the date the instrument is received by the Secretary of State unless the instrument provides that it is to be withheld from filing until a future date... The Secretary of State shall file a document as of any requested future date not more than 90 days after its receipt, including a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, if the document is received in the Secretary of State’s office at least one business day prior to the requested date of filing."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 110(a), California General Corporation Law, requesting a future filing date (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=110.)
  "Any instrument filed with respect to a corporation, other than original articles or instruments filed pursuant to Section 119, may provide that it is to become effective not more than 90 days subsequent to its filing date. In case such a delayed effective date is specified, the instrument may be prevented from becoming effective by a certificate stating that by appropriate corporate action it has been revoked and is null and void, executed in the same manner as the original instrument and filed before the specified effective date."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 110(c), California General Corporation Law, delayed effective date excludes original articles (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=110.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what timing options one real state's corporate-filing mechanics allow — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and delayed-filing or delayed-effectiveness options for a formation filing vary by state. This is also a genuine, important correction to an assumption worth stating plainly: a premise treating Cal. Corp. Code § 110's 'delayed effective date' option as available for a corporation's original articles turns out to be wrong on the current statutory text. Subdivision (c) — the actual 'delayed effective date' provision — explicitly carves original articles out of its own scope. A corporation's original articles can still have their filing date pushed out, but only through the different mechanism in subdivision (a) — asking the Secretary of State to withhold the document from filing until a requested future date — not through subdivision (c)'s delayed-effective-date option. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 110, and are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

INCORPORATOR SIGNATURE
Executed by the incorporator:

Incorporator: Jordan Alex Lee

Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

expectedJSON.body: California's general naming statute for corporations does not, by default, require a corporation's name to include any particular word like "Corporation," "Incorporated," "Limited," or an abbreviation of one of those words — that designator requirement applies only to a corporation that elects to be governed by the state's close-corporation provisions. What the general naming statute actually restricts is different: the Secretary of State will not file articles using a name containing "bank," "trust," "trustee," or related words unless a specified financial regulator's certificate of approval is attached, and separately, a corporation's name cannot be one the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public, or that isn't distinguishable in the Secretary of State's records from other registered or reserved entity names.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the bank/trust name restriction
citations.quote: The Secretary of State shall not file articles setting forth a name in which “bank,” “ trust,” “trustee,” or related words appear, unless the certificate of approval of the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation is attached thereto.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the misleading-name and distinguishability requirement
citations.quote: The name of a corporation shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public and shall be distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State from all of the following: (1) The name of any corporation. (2) The name of any foreign corporation authorized to transact intrastate business in this state.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the designator requirement is close-corporation-specific
citations.quote: The name of the corporation; provided, however, that in order for the corporation to be subject to the provisions of this division applicable to a close corporation (Section 158), the name of the corporation must contain the word “corporation,” “incorporated,” or “limited” or an abbreviation of one of such words.

That statute requires the agent to be either a natural person residing in California — whose complete business or residence street address must be stated — or a corporation that has separately qualified to act as a registered corporate agent, in which case no address for that corporate agent is included in the filing.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, agent for service of process named in the articles

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, who may serve as agent for service of process
citations.quote: The statement required by subdivision (a) shall also designate, as the agent of the corporation for the purpose of service of process, a natural person residing in this state or a corporation that has complied with Section 1505 and whose capacity to act as an agent has not terminated. If a natural person is designated, the statement shall set forth that person’s complete business or residence street address. If a corporate agent is designated, no address for it shall be set forth.

expectedJSON.body: Filing articles of incorporation does not end a corporation's filing obligations to the state. California requires every corporation to file an initial statement of information with the Secretary of State within 90 days after its articles are filed, and then again every year thereafter during the corporation's assigned filing period (or, if nothing has changed, to certify that no changes have occurred in lieu of refiling). The statement must report the corporation's name and Secretary of State file number, the names and addresses of its incumbent directors and any board vacancies, the names and addresses of its chief executive officer, secretary, and chief financial officer, its principal and mailing office addresses, the general type of business it conducts, its current agent for service of process, and a disclosure of whether any officer or director has an outstanding, non-appealable wage-order or Labor Code judgment against them.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, initial and annual statement of information
citations.quote: Every corporation shall file, within 90 days after the filing of its original articles and annually thereafter during the applicable filing period, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State, a statement containing all of the following: (1) The name of the corporation and the Secretary of State’s file number. (2) The names and complete business or residence addresses of its incumbent directors. (3) The number of vacancies on the board, if any. (4) The names and complete business or residence addresses of its chief executive officer, secretary, and chief financial officer. (5) The street address of its principal executive office.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, how the annual filing period is measured
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, the applicable filing period for a corporation shall be the calendar month during which its original articles were filed and the immediately preceding five calendar months. The Secretary of State shall provide a notice to each corporation to comply with this section approximately three months prior to the close of the applicable filing period... The failure of the corporation to receive the notice is not an excuse for failure to comply with this section.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's periodic-reporting requirement for corporations, not a claim about what any other state requires after formation — whether a follow-up report is required at all, and how often, varies by state. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 1502, and are treated as one source; no additional independent source was found for this. One distinction worth flagging precisely because this project's existing LLC Articles of Organization document describes a similar-sounding filing: the corporate version of this requirement recurs annually, while the parallel LLC statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.09) sets a biennial, every-two-year filing period — these are different cadences, and this corporate document should not be read as describing the LLC timeline.

expectedJSON.body: Incorporating in California also triggers a state tax obligation separate from the Secretary of State's filing fee. California's Revenue and Taxation Code subjects every corporation incorporated under California law to the state's minimum franchise tax — currently eight hundred dollars ($800) annually — running from the earlier of the date of incorporation, qualification, or first doing business in the state, until the corporation's dissolution or withdrawal becomes effective. Separately, that same statute exempts a newly incorporated corporation from the minimum franchise tax for its first taxable year, applicable to any corporation that incorporates or qualifies to do business in California on or after January 1, 2000 — with that first-year exemption expressly not extending to LLCs, limited partnerships, LLPs, or several other listed entity types.

citations.cite: The Corporation Franchise Tax, when the minimum tax applies
citations.quote: Every corporation described in subdivision (b) shall be subject to the minimum franchise tax specified in subdivision (d) from the earlier of the date of incorporation, qualification, or commencing to do business within this state, until the effective date of dissolution or withdrawal as provided in Section 23331 or, if later, the date the corporation ceases to do business within the limits of this state.

citations.cite: The Corporation Franchise Tax, the $800 minimum franchise tax amount
citations.quote: Except as provided in paragraph (2), paragraph (1) of subdivision (f) of Section 23151, paragraph (1) of subdivision (f) of Section 23181, and paragraph (1) of subdivision (c) of Section 23183, corporations subject to the minimum franchise tax shall pay annually to the state a minimum franchise tax of eight hundred dollars ($800).

citations.cite: The Corporation Franchise Tax, the permanent first-year exemption and its exclusions
citations.quote: (1) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), every corporation that incorporates or qualifies to do business in this state on or after January 1, 2000, shall not be subject to the minimum franchise tax for its first taxable year. (2) This subdivision shall not apply to limited partnerships, as defined in Section 17935, limited liability companies, as defined in Section 17941, limited liability partnerships, as described in Section 17948, charitable organizations, as described in Section 23703, regulated investment companies, as defined in Section 851 of the Internal Revenue Code, real estate investment trusts, as defined in Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code, real estate mortgage investment conduits, as defined in Section 860D of the Internal Revenue Code, and qualified Subchapter S subsidiaries, as defined in Section 1361(b)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code, to the extent applicable.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's minimum annual corporate tax, not a claim about what any other state charges — whether a state imposes a flat annual tax on corporations at all, and in what amount, varies by state. This clause also corrects an assumption worth checking rather than carrying over from this project's existing LLC research: the LLC Articles of Organization document describes a first-year exemption from the $800 minimum tax that was temporary, applying only to LLCs organizing between January 1, 2021 and January 1, 2024 (Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941(g)). The corporation first-year exemption verified here is a different, older provision found in effect as of this verification date with no stated end date in this section — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(f)(1), covering any corporation that incorporates or qualifies to do business in California on or after January 1, 2000. These are not the same exemption extended to a second entity type; they are separately worded, separately dated provisions in different statutory sections that happen to produce a similar-looking result, and by its own terms the corporate exemption does not reach LLCs or several other listed entity types. The three quotes below come from subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153, and are treated as one source, not three independent ones.

expectedJSON.body: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(b) defines the corporations the minimum franchise tax reaches, unless expressly exempted elsewhere in the Corporation Tax Law or by the California Constitution: a corporation incorporated under California law, a corporation qualified to transact intrastate business in California under the Corporations Code, or a corporation doing business in California. Section 23153(c) then carves two entity types out of the tax entirely: credit unions, and a narrow category of agricultural nonprofit cooperative associations organized under the Food and Agricultural Code and holding a specified board-of-supervisors certificate, which are exempt for five consecutive taxable years starting with the year the certificate issued -- and only if the cooperative organized on or after January 1, 1994. Limited liability companies are not reached by this section directly; a separate statute, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941, imposes an annual LLC tax and cross-references subdivision (d) of this section only to set that tax's dollar amount.

citations.cite: The Corporation Franchise Tax, which corporations the minimum tax applies to
citations.quote: Unless expressly exempted by this part or the California Constitution, subdivision (a) shall apply to each of the following: (1) Every corporation that is incorporated under the laws of this state. (2) Every corporation that is qualified to transact intrastate business in this state pursuant to Chapter 21 (commencing with Section 2100) of Division 1 of Title 1 of the Corporations Code. (3) Every corporation that is doing business in this state.

citations.cite: The Corporation Franchise Tax, express exemptions for credit unions and certain agricultural cooperatives
citations.quote: The following entities are not subject to the minimum franchise tax specified in this section: (1) Credit unions. (2) Nonprofit cooperative associations organized pursuant to Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 54001) of Division 20 of the Food and Agricultural Code that have been issued the certificate of the board of supervisors prepared pursuant to Section 54042 of the Food and Agricultural Code. The association shall be exempt from the minimum franchise tax for five consecutive taxable years, commencing with the first taxable year for which the certificate is issued pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 54042 of the Food and Agricultural Code. This paragraph only applies to nonprofit cooperative associations organized on or after January 1, 1994.

expectedJSON.body: California's general corporate-filing statute gives a corporation two different, non-interchangeable ways to time when a filed document takes effect. First, under the ordinary filing-date rule, the person filing any instrument — including the original articles of incorporation — may ask the Secretary of State to withhold it from filing until a specified future date up to 90 days after the Secretary of State receives it, so long as the document actually arrives at least one business day before that requested date; if honored, the filing date itself becomes that later date. Second, and separately, the statute lets a corporation specify that an instrument is to become effective up to 90 days after its filing date, rather than immediately upon filing — but that second, 'delayed effective date' mechanism is expressly unavailable for original articles of incorporation; the statute limits it to instruments filed with respect to a corporation that already exists.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, requesting a future filing date
citations.quote: Except for instruments filed pursuant to Section 1502, the date of filing shall be the date the instrument is received by the Secretary of State unless the instrument provides that it is to be withheld from filing until a future date... The Secretary of State shall file a document as of any requested future date not more than 90 days after its receipt, including a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, if the document is received in the Secretary of State’s office at least one business day prior to the requested date of filing.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, delayed effective date excludes original articles
citations.quote: Any instrument filed with respect to a corporation, other than original articles or instruments filed pursuant to Section 119, may provide that it is to become effective not more than 90 days subsequent to its filing date. In case such a delayed effective date is specified, the instrument may be prevented from becoming effective by a certificate stating that by appropriate corporate action it has been revoked and is null and void, executed in the same manner as the original instrument and filed before the specified effective date.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what timing options one real state's corporate-filing mechanics allow — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and delayed-filing or delayed-effectiveness options for a formation filing vary by state. This is also a genuine, important correction to an assumption worth stating plainly: a premise treating Cal. Corp. Code § 110's 'delayed effective date' option as available for a corporation's original articles turns out to be wrong on the current statutory text. Subdivision (c) — the actual 'delayed effective date' provision — explicitly carves original articles out of its own scope. A corporation's original articles can still have their filing date pushed out, but only through the different mechanism in subdivision (a) — asking the Secretary of State to withhold the document from filing until a requested future date — not through subdivision (c)'s delayed-effective-date option. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 110, and are treated as one source, not two independent ones.
